items.title: Tripartite Struggle — What, Why & Who
items.body:
## The contest for Kannauj

- The **Tripartite Struggle** (also **Kannauj Triangle Wars**) was a two-century (8th-9th c.) contest among three dynasties for the city of **Kannauj**:
  - **Palas** of Bengal-Bihar
  - **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of Avanti
  - **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan
- It followed the **decline of Harsha's empire** (mid-7th c.), which left a power vacuum in northern India with no central authority.

## Why Kannauj?

| Motive | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Strategic/trade | Sat on the **Ganga trade route** — a hub of lucrative markets |
| Legitimacy | Former **capital of Harsha**; holding it conferred prestige |
| Economic | Trade revenues funded military and administrative power |
| Prestige titles | Winner claimed **Sakalottarapathanatha / Uttarapathaswami** ('Lord of North India') |
keyPoints: Tripartite Struggle = Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas contesting Kannauj across the 8th-9th centuries.
It arose from the power vacuum left by the decline of Harsha's empire.
Kannauj was prized for its Ganga trade-route wealth and its legitimacy as Harsha's old capital.
The winner claimed the title Sakalottarapathanatha / Uttarapathaswami — Lord of North India.

items.title: The Three Contenders at a Glance
items.body:
## Profiles of the rival dynasties

| Dynasty | Base | Founder | Peak ruler | Signature legacy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pala** (750-1161) | Bengal & Bihar | Gopala (elected) | Dharmapala / Devapala | Vikramshila University; revived Nalanda; Buddhist patronage |
| **Gurjara-Pratihara** (730-1036) | Avanti (from Mandor) | — | Mihira Bhoja | Checked Arab expansion; epithet 'Ranahastina' |
| **Rashtrakuta** (753-982) | Deccan | Dantidurga | Govinda III | Kailasa temple, Ellora; Kannada literature |

## Points to remember

- **Gopala** of the Palas was **elected** by local feudal lords — a notable exception to hereditary kingship.
- **Dharmapala** founded **Vikramshila** and revived **Nalanda**, making the Palas the great Buddhist patrons of the east.
- The **Pratiharas** rose from the **Mandor** region (near Jodhpur) and are credited with **checking the Arab advance** from Sindh.
- The **Rashtrakutas** repeatedly intervened from the Deccan (Dhruva, Govinda III) but were always pulled back home.
keyPoints: Pala founder Gopala was elected; Dharmapala founded Vikramshila and revived Nalanda.
The Palas were the leading Buddhist patrons of Bengal and Bihar.
Gurjara-Pratiharas rose from Mandor; Mihira Bhoja checked the Arabs and they were called 'Ranahastina'.
Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga and built the Kailasa temple at Ellora.

items.title: Phases, Battles & Outcome
items.body:
## How the struggle unfolded

- **Phase I (c. 790-810):** **Vatsaraja (Pratihara)** defeated **Dharmapala (Pala)** at Prayag, but was then beaten by **Dhruva I (Rashtrakuta)**, who could not consolidate because of Deccan conflicts. Kannauj changed hands repeatedly.
- **Phase II (c. 810-836):** **Nagabhata II (Pratihara)** captured Kannauj from the Pala vassal **Chakrayudha** and beat Dharmapala; **Govinda III (Rashtrakuta)** defeated Nagabhata II but withdrew to the Deccan. By the late 9th century the **Pratiharas** emerged as the leading northern power.

## Consequences

- **Political fragmentation** — no lasting central authority in the north.
- **Economic strain** — constant warfare drained all three, especially the Palas and Rashtrakutas.
- **Cultural output** — temple styles (Nagara/Vesara), revival of Nalanda, Kannada literature under the Rashtrakutas.
- **Decline of the Pratiharas** — external threats (Mahmud of Ghazni) plus internal breakup led to the rise of independent **Rajput states**, later overrun by the **Ghurids**.
keyPoints: Phase I: Vatsaraja beat Dharmapala but lost to Dhruva; Kannauj kept changing hands.
Phase II: Nagabhata II captured Kannauj from Chakrayudha; Govinda III won but withdrew to the Deccan.
The Pratiharas emerged as the leading northern power by the late 9th century.
The struggle drained all three powers and left north India politically fragmented.
Pratihara decline gave rise to independent Rajput states later overrun by the Ghurids.

items.title: Rise of the Rajput States after the Pratiharas
items.body:
## The successor kingdoms

With the Gurjara-Pratihara empire breaking up, several Rajput dynasties became independent in the 10th-12th centuries.

| Dynasty | Region / capital | Notable ruler | Cultural legacy |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chandellas** | Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand); Khajuraho, Kalanjara, Mahoba | Dhanga; Vidyadhar (took Kanauj 1018) | **Khajuraho** temples — Kandariya Mahadev |
| **Paramaras** | Malwa; Dharanagar (Dhar) | **Bhoja** (1010-55) | **Bhojpur** & Bhojeshwar Temple; scholar-king |
| **Chaulukyas / Solankis** | Gujarat; Anhilawada (Patan) | Jaisimha Siddharaja; Kumarpala | **Maru-Gurjara** style — Modhera Sun Temple, Rani-ki-Vav |

## Extra recall

- **Somnath Temple** was plundered by **Mahmud of Ghazni** during **Bhimadeva I's** reign (1025 CE).
- **Rani-ki-Vav** at Patan, built by Queen Udayamati, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
- The **agnikula myth** traces clans such as the Pratiharas, Chauhans, Paramaras and Solankis to a fire-pit sacrifice at Mount Abu.
keyPoints: Chandellas ruled Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) and built Khajuraho, including the Kandariya Mahadev temple.
Paramara Bhoja ruled from Dharanagar (Dhar) and built Bhojpur and the Bhojeshwar Temple.
Solankis (Chaulukyas) of Gujarat ruled from Anhilawada (Patan) and built the Modhera Sun Temple and Rani-ki-Vav.
Somnath was plundered by Mahmud of Ghazni under Bhimadeva I in 1025 CE.
The agnikula myth derives several Rajput clans from a fire-pit sacrifice at Mount Abu.

items.title: Chauhans, Gahadavalas, Tomaras & the Tarain Battles
items.body:
## The last Rajput powers before the Sultanate

- **Tomaras of Delhi:** ruled around Dhillika (Delhi) from the 10th c.; **Anangpal Tomar** built **Lal Kot**. Delhi later passed to the **Chauhans** under Vigrahraja.
- **Chauhans (Chahmanas) of Ajmer:** began as Pratihara feudatories; **Ajayaraja** founded **Ajayameru (Ajmer)**. **Prithviraj III (Rai Pithora)** became the most famous ruler.
- **Gahadavalas of Kannauj:** ruled Kannauj and Varanasi (1090-1193); **Govindachandra** brought them to their peak; **Jaichandra** was the last great ruler.

## The Tarain Battles

| Battle | Year | Result |
|---|---|---|
| First Tarain | 1191 CE | Prithviraj III **defeats** Muhammad Ghori |
| Second Tarain | 1192 CE | Ghori **defeats** Prithviraj — Chauhan power collapses |

- **Jaichandra** died fighting the Ghurids (Chandawar, 1194); Kannauj later fell to Iltutmish.
- **Literary sources:** **'Prithviraj Vijaya'** (Jayanaka) is the reliable contemporary account; **'Prithviraj Raso'** (Chand Bardai), written later, alleges Jaichandra invited Ghori — unconfirmed by any inscription.
keyPoints: Anangpal Tomar built Lal Kot at Delhi; the Chauhans later took Delhi.
Chauhan Ajayaraja founded Ajmer; Prithviraj III was the most famous Chauhan king.
First Battle of Tarain (1191): Prithviraj wins; Second Battle of Tarain (1192): Ghori wins.
Gahadavala Govindachandra brought the dynasty to its peak; Jaichandra died fighting the Ghurids in 1194.
Prithviraj Vijaya (Jayanaka) is reliable; Prithviraj Raso (Chand Bardai) is a later, unverified account.
items.mnemonic: Tarain: '91 Prithviraj, '92 Ghori — the loser of the second battle lost India.
